summary: Describes considerations for mailing lists when non-ASCII UTF-8 email addresses are introduced. It outlines possible scenarios for lists that mix non-ASCII and traditional addresses, but does not specify protocol changes or offer implementation or deployment advice. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Mailing lists send one letter to many people. This memo thinks through what happens when some addresses use letters from other alphabets and some do not.

questions: mailing lists with internationalized email addresses
utf-8 email addresses on mailing lists
mixing ascii and non-ascii list members
how do mailing lists downgrade headers
subtitle: What mailing lists have to think about when some subscribers use non-ASCII UTF-8 email addresses.

tldr.problem: Mailing lists redistribute one message to many people. Once some addresses contain non-ASCII UTF-8 characters, lists must handle transport, headers and policy for subscribers who may or may not be able to receive such mail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes scenarios (fully SMTPUTF8 lists and mixed lists), envelope issues and the problems of List-* headers and downgraded messages. It specifies no protocol changes.
tldr.outcome: It is Informational and obsoletes RFC 5983. It offers considerations and possible work-arounds, not implementation or deployment advice.

facts.label: Security considerations
facts.value: None beyond what mailing list agents do now

today: RFC 6783 is Informational and obsoletes RFC 5983. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Mailing Lists and Non-ASCII Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 6783 looks at what internationalized email addresses, as described in RFC 6530, mean for mailing lists. It names three affected areas: transport (receiving and sending messages), message headers of received and retransmitted messages, and mailing list operational policies.

A mailing list agent, usually software, receives a message at one address and redistributes it. It usually changes the envelope return address (the 'bounce address') so that errors go to the list agent instead of the original sender. The agent normally resubmits the message as a new one using message submission, per RFC 6409. Lists implemented as an expansion step inside one SMTP transaction are not covered.

The RFC points out that a list sender often does not know who the members are or whether they can receive SMTPUTF8 mail, so remedies that work for one-to-one mail may not be available. It splits list internationalization into three questions: does the list have a non-ASCII submission address, does it accept non-ASCII subscriptions, and does it accept messages that require SMTPUTF8.
sections.eli5: A mailing list is like a teacher photocopying one note for the whole class. The trouble starts when some kids can only read one kind of writing.

sections.title: Scenarios: Fully SMTPUTF8 and Mixed Lists
sections.content:
A fully SMTPUTF8 list expects every subscriber to be able to receive SMTPUTF8 mail. A non-ASCII subscriber address must be able to, but for an ASCII address there is no way to tell short of sending a probe or confirmation message and finding out whether it was delivered, for instance if the user clicked a link in it.

A mixed list handles both kinds of subscribers, either as a transition or permanently. Downgrading SMTPUTF8 mail to ASCII is not possible in general, but list software might split recipients into two sets and send a downgraded copy to the ASCII set. To choose the set, the software might conservatively assume ASCII addresses get ASCII messages, probe with a test message, or let the subscriber choose, much as lists let users pick plain text or HTML.

On the SMTP side, the bounce address usually includes the list name, so a list with a non-ASCII name has a non-ASCII bounce address. List software might use an ASCII bounce address instead to make bounces more likely to return. The same goes for per-recipient bounce addresses (VERP), which embed the subscriber's address.
sections.eli5: Some lists only talk to people who read the new writing. Others have to keep two piles of notes: one in the new writing and one in the plain old kind.

sections.title: List Headers and Downgrading
sections.content:
List agents add headers such as List-Id, List-Help, List-Unsubscribe, List-Subscribe, List-Post, List-Owner and List-Archive. They come from RFC 2369 and RFC 2919, which were written before SMTPUTF8 and permit only ASCII, including in URLs. Even when a URI scheme allows an internationalized form, the RFC says it should use the pure ASCII form of RFC 3986, so non-ASCII characters can only be included by encoding them as ASCII.

That encoding is percent-encoding, which has a catch: percent signs were used informally in addresses for source routing, so some mail software forbids or escapes them. Extending List-Id to non-ASCII would also be awkward, since filters might not compare encoded and unencoded values correctly, and ASCII encodings are hard for users to type.

When downgrading a message, all List-* headers must be downgraded. A non-ASCII mailto may need editing out or replacing with an ASCII equivalent. A downgraded List-Id may no longer be recognizable as the same list. MIME file names and descriptive strings may lose their sense, and the From: address of a non-ASCII submitter cannot be preserved so ASCII recipients can reply. Possible work-arounds, none known to be implemented, are an alternate ASCII address registered with the list, ASCII forwarding addresses created by the list, or putting the list address in From:.
sections.eli5: If you must rewrite a note in plain letters, some names turn into gibberish. Then the person who gets it may not know who sent it or how to write back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security section is a single line: 'None beyond what mailing list agents do now.' The RFC introduces no new protocol and so identifies no new security issues of its own.

It is also explicit about what it does not do. As its abstract says, it outlines possible scenarios for handling lists with mixtures of non-ASCII and traditional addresses but does not specify protocol changes or offer implementation or deployment advice.
sections.eli5: This memo only thinks out loud, so it adds no new ways for bad things to happen.
